nameStory: The 'narrow-leaved' part is pretty straightforward - this plant has slender leaflets that distinguish it from its broad-leaved cousin. The 'everlasting-pea' name comes from its perennial nature and showy pea-like flowers that seem to bloom endlessly through summer. Unlike true garden peas that die after one season, this wild relative keeps coming back year after year.
description: Narrow-leaved everlasting-pea is a sprawling perennial vine that forms dense mats of greenery along roadsides and field edges. This member of the pea family climbs and scrambles using tendrils, reaching several feet in length. Its most striking feature is the cluster of bright pink pea-shaped flowers that bloom throughout summer. The plant has distinctive winged stems and pairs of narrow leaflets that help it stand out from other wild peas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink pea-shaped flowers cluster together on long stems, each bloom about an inch across with the classic 'butterfly' shape of a banner petal above smaller wing and keel petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Each leaf consists of just two narrow, elongated leaflets that feel smooth and somewhat thick, ending in branched tendrils that help the plant climb

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctive flattened, winged stems that feel angular rather than round when you roll them between your fingers - a key identifying feature

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat brown pods about 2 inches long that split open with a slight 'pop' when ripe, revealing several round peas inside

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms sprawling mats that climb over other vegetation using tendrils, often creating dense tangles several feet across

habitat: Look for narrow-leaved everlasting-pea along roadsides, field edges, and disturbed areas throughout New England. It thrives in sunny spots with well-drained soil and often grows along fences, stone walls, and woodland borders where it can climb over other vegetation. This adaptable plant tolerates poor soils and is commonly found scrambling up embankments and through tall grass in abandoned lots.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the distinctive winged stems begin to sprawl, with the characteristic two-leaflet leaves unfurling. Tendrils start reaching for nearby plants to climb.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright pink flowers appearing in clusters from June through August. Pods begin forming as flowers fade, and the plant reaches its full sprawling size.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open, scattering peas for next year's growth. Foliage begins to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, but the perennial root system survives underground, ready to send up new shoots in spring.

funFact: This plant is actually a bit of a botanical escape artist - it was originally introduced from Europe as a potential forage crop but 'broke free' from cultivation and now thrives in the wild, proving sometimes the best way to succeed is to go rogue!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with broad-leaved sweet pea, but remember 'narrow vs. broad' - if the leaflets are skinny like green beans, you've got narrow-leaved everlasting-pea; if they're wide like garden pea leaves, it's the broad-leaved species. The winged stems are also more pronounced in the narrow-leaved variety.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'everlasting-pea,' this isn't closely related to the sweet peas sold at florist shops, and you shouldn't eat the pods - unlike garden peas, wild peas can contain compounds that aren't good for you. The 'everlasting' refers to its perennial nature, not any preservative qualities.
compareHints: Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems. Seaside pea has purple flowers and grows on beaches, while meadow pea has yellow blooms. The two-leaflet arrangement also distinguishes it from vetches, which typically have many more leaflets per leaf.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat.
Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets.
Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms.
Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers.

Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system.
Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea.
Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color.
